newsitem.title: USA: Panel named to study reshaping U.S. military.
newsitem.headline: Panel named to study reshaping U.S. military.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen on Thursday appointed a nine-member panel of experts headed by Philip Odeen, President of BDM International Inc., to look at reshaping the U.S. military for the 21st century.

The National Defence Panel, selected in consultations with Congress, will help the Pentagon examine changes in the U.S. defence posture as budgets are reduced after the collapse of the former Soviet Union.

Reshaping defence, including possible cuts in troop strength below 1.44 million to pay for weapons modernisation, has become a critical issue as military spending is reduced to balance the federal budget.

The panel will review and make final recommendations to Cohen by May 15 on the Pentagon's ongoing Quadrennial Defence Review (QDR) and provide an assessment by year's end of alternative U.S. force structures through 2010.

Among issues that will be addressed in the QDR and by the panel is whether the U.S. military should retain its policy of being prepared to fight and win two major regional military conflicts virtually at once.

Panel members in addition to Odeen are former Assistant Defence Secretary Richard Armitage, retired Marine Gen. Richard Hearney, retired Navy Adm. David Jeremiah -- a former vice chairman of the joint Chiefs of Staff -- and Managing Director Robert Kimmitt of Lehman Brothers investment bankers.

Others are Director Andrew Krepinevich of the Centre for Strategic and Budgetary Assessments, retired Air Force Gen. James McCarthy, military analyst Janne Nonlan of the Brookings Institution and retired Army Gen. Robert RisCassi who is vice president of land systems for Lockheed Martin Corp.

The QDR, similar to a "bottom-up" defence review four years ago, comes at a time when the military is being called upon not only to be ready to fight two wars at once but to take part in peacekeeping and routine "forward-presence" operations around the world.

Announcement of the new panel came as President Bill Clinton sent Congress a $265 billion 1998 defence budget that was expected to spark a battle with Republicans who say military spending has fallen dangerously since the Cold War.

Deputy Defence Secretary John White told reporters in December that the QDR would look at everything from strategy to troops strength and weaponary in order to field a force that can support U.S. policy with lower defence spending.
"Everything is on the table," White said.
